title: Greedy Vertex Placement
content: The core greedy step: for vertex $k$ with current partition $S$, compute the total edge weight from $k$ to vertices in $S$ and to vertices in $S^c$. If the weight to $S^c$ is at least as large, insert $k$ into $S$ (so its edges to $S^c$ are cut). Otherwise, leave $k$ in $S^c$ (so its edges to $S$ are cut). In either case, the vertex is placed opposite to where it has more connections, maximizing cut contribution.
mathContext: $\text{greedyStep}(G, S, k) = \begin{cases} S \cup \{k\} & \text{if } \sum_{j \in S^c} w(k,j) \geq \sum_{j \in S} w(k,j) \\ S & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$

title: Full Greedy Partition Construction
content: The greedy partition is constructed by folding `greedyStep` over all vertices in `Fin n`, starting from the empty set. This processes vertices in canonical order $0, 1, \ldots, n-1$, placing each one greedily. The use of `Multiset.foldl` on `Finset.univ.val` provides a deterministic ordering. This is the constructive content that replaces the existential axiom from the parent file.

title: Greedy Contribution Function
content: The contribution of vertex $k$ to the cut is the maximum of the edge weight from $k$ to $S$ and to $S^c$. Since the greedy algorithm always picks the side that maximizes cut contribution, the actual cut contribution equals this maximum. This definition is the bridge between the algorithm and the lower bound analysis.
mathContext: $\text{greedyContrib}(G, S, k) = \max\left(\sum_{j \in S} w(k,j),\, \sum_{j \in S^c} w(k,j)\right)$

title: The Key Inequality: max ≥ average
content: This elegant two-line proof is the mathematical heart of the entire derandomization. By case-splitting on $a \leq b$ vs $a > b$, the result follows immediately from `linarith`. Though simple, this inequality captures why greedy is at least as good as random: a random choice achieves $(a+b)/2$ in expectation, while the greedy choice achieves $\max(a,b) \geq (a+b)/2$.

title: Each Greedy Step Achieves ≥ Half
content: Applies `max_ge_avg` to the two sums of edge weights from vertex $k$ to $S$ and $S^c$. The nonnegativity preconditions are discharged via `Finset.sum_nonneg` and the weight nonnegativity axiom of the weighted graph. This is the per-vertex guarantee that sums to the global $W/2$ bound.
mathContext: $\text{greedyContrib}(G, S, k) \geq \frac{\sum_{j \in S} w(k,j) + \sum_{j \in S^c} w(k,j)}{2}$

title: Weight Sum Partitions Over S and S^c
content: The edge weights from vertex $k$ to all other vertices decompose as the sum over $S$ plus the sum over $S^c$. This follows from the fact that $S$ and $S^c$ are disjoint and their union is the universe. The result uses `Finset.sum_union` with `disjoint_compl_right`.

title: Toggle Involution for Subset Counting
content: A key combinatorial tool: `toggleElem j S` flips the membership of element $j$ in $S$. This is an involution (applying it twice returns the original set). By pairing each subset containing $j$ with the corresponding subset not containing $j$, we establish a bijection that proves exactly half of all subsets contain any given element. This is more elegant than the binomial coefficient argument and works directly in the Finset framework.
mathContext: $\text{toggle}_j(S) = \begin{cases} S \setminus \{j\} & j \in S \\ S \cup \{j\} & j \notin S \end{cases}$, with $\text{toggle}_j \circ \text{toggle}_j = \text{id}$

title: Half of All Subsets Contain a Given Element
content: Proves that exactly $2^{n-1}$ of the $2^n$ subsets of $\text{Fin}\, n$ contain a given element $i$. The proof uses the toggle involution to establish a bijection between subsets containing $i$ and those not containing $i$, then exploits the fact that these two families have equal cardinality and sum to $2^n$. This is a foundational counting lemma for the averaging argument.

title: Counting Subsets Separating Two Elements
content: For distinct elements $i, j$, exactly $2^{n-2}$ subsets contain $i$ but not $j$. The proof toggles $j$'s membership (preserving $i$'s membership since $i \neq j$) to biject between $\{i \in S, j \in S\}$ and $\{i \in S, j \notin S\}$. Since these two families partition the $2^{n-1}$ subsets containing $i$, each has size $2^{n-2}$. This is the key counting lemma: it says each edge $(i,j)$ is cut by exactly one-quarter of all partitions.

title: Cut Weight as Indicator Sum
content: Converts the cut weight from a sum over $S$ and $S^c$ to a sum over all vertex pairs $(i, j)$ with an indicator: $w(i,j)$ if $i \in S$ and $j \notin S$, and $0$ otherwise. This algebraic reformulation is crucial for swapping the summation order in the averaging identity.

title: The Averaging Identity: Sum of All Cut Weights
content: The crown jewel of the combinatorial argument: the sum of cut weights over all $2^n$ partitions equals $\text{totalWeight}(G) \cdot 2^{n-1}$. The proof swaps summation order (partitions $\leftrightarrow$ vertex pairs), applies the counting lemmas to evaluate each inner sum, uses the no-self-loops property to handle the diagonal, and performs careful arithmetic with powers of 2. This 70-line proof is the most technically demanding part of the formalization.

title: Main Theorem: Existence of a Good Partition
content: The culmination of the proof: for any weighted graph, there exists a partition with cut weight at least $W/2$. The proof applies `conditional_expectation_method` with the averaging identity: since the average cut weight over all $2^n$ partitions equals $W/2$ (from `sum_cutWeight_eq`), some partition must achieve at least $W/2$. This constructively eliminates the `exists_good_partition` axiom from `RandomizedMaxcutOQ02.lean`.

title: Concrete Example: Triangle Graph
content: A unit-weight triangle graph $K_3$ serves as a concrete test case. With total weight 3, any partition cuts at least 2 edges (weight $\geq 3/2 = 1.5$, achieved with weight 2). This illustrates that the $W/2$ bound is not always tight: the triangle achieves a 2/3 ratio, better than the guaranteed 1/2.
mathContext: $K_3$ with unit weights: $W = 3$, optimal cut weight $= 2 \geq 3/2$

title: Abstract Conditional Expectations Principle
content: The abstract probabilistic method: if the average of $f$ over a finite type is at least $c$, then some element achieves at least $c$. Proved by contradiction: if every $f(a) < c$, then the sum is strictly less than $|A| \cdot c$, contradicting the average hypothesis. This is the simplest non-trivial application of the probabilistic method, and serves as the template for Johnson's MAX-SAT algorithm, Spencer's derandomization framework, and many other results.
mathContext: $\frac{1}{|A|} \sum_{a \in A} f(a) \geq c \implies \exists a \in A: f(a) \geq c$
